Enhanced anaerobic digestion of rice straw by using microbial pretreatment 
augmented with micro-nano bubble water
Suyun Xu a,*, Yakun Lu a, Xuezhi Liu a, Ruixiang Zou a, Yuchen Zhang a,  
Mukesh Kumar Awasthi b, Hewen Wei c, Hongbo Liu a,*
a School of Environment and Architecture, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China
b College of Natural Resources and Environment, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, Shanxi Province, 712100, China
c Shanghai Microcre Optics-Mech Tech Co., Ltd, Shanghai, 201411, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Enzyme activity
Mixed microbial agent
Micro-nano bubbles
Methane production
Phanerodontia chrysosporium
A B S T R A C T
Micro-nano bubbles (MNBs) can enhance microbial processes, but their role in boosting defined microbial 
consortia for biomass pretreatment is unknown. This study demonstrates a novel pretreatment strategy that 
synergistically combines compound microbial consortia with MNBs to dramatically improve rice straw decom­
position and anaerobic digestion. The compound consortia were comprised of Bacillus velezensis HAB-2 (S1), 
Phanerodontia chrysosporium (S2), and Phanerodontia chrysosporium SILI (S3) at varied ratios. Based on straw 
degradation rate, hydrolysate sCOD, and methane production, the proportion of microbial consortia differen­
tially impacted the degradation of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Specifically, the K-1 (S1:S2:S3 = 1:1:1) 
and K-2 (S1:S2:S3 = 2:1:1) consortia showed the best synergistic effects. K-2 consortium with Air-MNBs achieved 
the highest degradation rates of total solids (TS, 43.5 %) and volatile solids (VS, 28.0 %), which increased 58.2 % 
and 86.7 %, respectively over controls without MNBs injection. Correspondingly, the K-2 consortium pretreated 
with Air-MNBs achieved a maximum methane yield of 47.5 mL/g VS, significantly higher than that of the un­
treated control group. Air-MNBs were more effective than N2-MNBs in bacterial pretreatment, whereas their 
enhancement in fungal pretreatment was not significant. This work establishes a new approach for enhancing 
lignocellulosic biomass pretreatment by harnessing the synergy between designed microbial consortia and MNBs 
technology.
1. Introduction
Biomass energy is a crucial renewable resource, and agricultural 
waste such as rice straw serves as an important biomass source (Wang 
et al., 2022). Globally, approximately one billion tons of straw are 
produced annually (Harun et al., 2022). Improper disposal not only 
wastes energy but also occupies space and causes environmental dam­
age. A promising solution is converting straw into biogas through 
anaerobic digestion (AD), which can help to alleviate energy shortages. 
As a lignocellulosic material, straw contains 32–47 % cellulose, 19–27 % 
hemicellulose, and 5–24 % lignin (Harun et al., 2022). Its recalcitrant 
structure, characterized by lignin encapsulation and silicified surfaces, 
hinders microbial degradation of cellulose and makes hydrolysis the 
rate-limiting step in AD (Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2015). Some studies 
have tried the utilization of the co-culture of microbial agents to 
enhance the degradation of rice straw, with the degradation rates of 
lignin and cellulose being 26.38 % and 33.29 %, respectively (Chen 
et al., 2019). However, achieving a high and cost-effective degradation 
rate of lignocellulose in straw to substantially boost biogas production 
remains a significant challenge.
Micro-nano bubbles (MNBs), defined as bubbles with diameters 
below 100 μm, exhibit unique properties such as prolonged stability, 
high specific surface area, and efficient mass transfer (Xiao et al., 2025). 
Aeration with MNBs increases dissolved oxygen levels, supporting mi­
crobial growth and organic pollutant degradation (Lyu et al., 2019). The 
high zeta potential of MNBs enhances particle dispersion and substrate 
accessibility, thereby improving methane production (Chuenchart et al., 
2021; Hou et al., 2024). Furthermore, MNBs influence enzyme activity 
through surface charge interactions and generation of hydroxyl radicals 
(•OH) during collapse, which may alter enzyme conformation or redox 
state (Yamaguchi et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017). The sustained oxygen 
release also promotes aerobic microbial metabolism and associated

enzymatic pathways, underscoring the dual role of MNBs as physical and 
biochemical modulators in enzyme-mediated processes (Silva et al., 
2024).
Biological pretreatment using microbial consortia represents a 
promising avenue for enhancing lignocellulose deconstruction. The 
synergy between fungal and bacterial members in composite microbial 
agents can lead to more effective degradation of straw components than 
single strains. This is evidenced by recent studies; for instance, a defined 
microbial consortium was reported to increase cellulolytic enzyme ac­
tivities significantly and achieve a 45.9 % enhancement in biogas pro­
duction from rice straw (Sahil et al., 2023). Furthermore, the 
combination of biological and physicochemical pretreatments has been 
shown to be a highly effective strategy. For instance, the integration of 
ultrasonic pretreatment with bioaugmentation achieved the highest 
methane production and significantly enhanced the crude cellulose 
removal rate during anaerobic digestion, demonstrating a clear syner­
gistic effect (Zhang et al., 2023). Despite these advances, biological 
pretreatment efficiency is often hampered by intrinsic limitations 
including slow mass transfer and suboptimal microbial synergy within 
the consortia.
Concurrently, MNBs technology has demonstrated considerable po­
tential in enhancing AD processes. Its application has been shown to 
substantially improve methane yield from various organic wastes. For 
example, adding Air-/H₂-/CO₂-nanobubble water to swine manure 
digestion increased cumulative methane production by 19–39 %, 
attributed to accelerated hydrolysis of proteins/carbohydrates and 
enhanced enzyme activity (Fan et al., 2020). In the context of waste 
activated sludge, supplementation with N2-nanobubble water boosted 
methane yield by 29 %, which was mechanistically linked to a 14–17 % 
increase in the activities of key extracellular hydrolases (Yang et al., 
2019). Critically, while MNBs have been used within the digestion phase 
or as a soaking agent (Wang et al., 2023), their potential to specifically 
augment a dedicated microbial pretreatment stage has been completely 
overlooked. This represents a key strategic gap. We posit that using 
MNBs to create an optimized microenvironment during pretreatment 
can powerfully amplify the synergy and enzymatic activity of inoculated 
consortia.
It is hypothesized that the unique properties of MNBs (e.g., high mass 
transfer, reactive oxygen species generation, and zeta potential modu­
lation) can create a superior micro-environment that amplifies the ac­
tivity and synergy of pre-inoculated, specialized consortia. To bridge 
this gap, this study systematically investigates the synergistic effects of 
combining specifically formulated microbial consortia (Bacillus vele­
zensis and Phanerodontia chrysosporium at different ratios) with different 
types of MNBs water (Air vs. N2) for pretreating rice straw. The objec­
tives are to: (1) evaluate the enhancement in straw decomposition ef­
ficiency; (2) elucidate the underlying mechanisms through enzyme 
activity profiling; and (3) determine the ultimate impact on biomethane 
production. This work is distinguished by three key innovations: (1) We 
are the first to employ MNBs as a dedicated enhancer for a standalone 
microbial pretreatment stage, rather than as a direct additive to anaer­
obic digestion. (2) We systematically investigate the interaction be­
tween specifically formulated bacterial-fungal consortia and different 
types of MNBs (Air vs. N₂). (3) We move beyond performance metrics to 
elucidate the underlying mechanisms through extracellular enzyme ac­
tivity profiling.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Screening of strains
The substrate for AD was rice straw, which was air-dried and ground 
to an average particle size of 1–2 cm before use. The anaerobic inoculum 
was digested sludge obtained from a full-scale mesophilic biogas plant 
(Ouhai Energy Co., Ltd., Chongming District, Shanghai, China). To 
minimize endogenous gas production, the inoculum was pre-incubated 
at 37 ◦C in the laboratory until gas production ceased, and then stored 
at 4 ◦C prior to use. The fundamental physicochemical properties of the 
rice straw and inoculum were characterized, and the detailed data are 
provided in Table S1 (Supplementary Information).
The bacterial strains were isolated from compost samples using a 
cellulose-Congo red medium to screen for cellulose-degrading ability 
(Mathews et al., 2014). The screened strains were further isolated, pu­
rified, and expanded in culture. Subsequently, they were identified by 
16S rDNA and ITS sequencing. Strain S1 was identified as belonging to 
the genus Bacillus, showing 100 % similarity to Bacillus velezensis strain 
HAB-2. Strains S2 and S3 were identified as belonging to the genus 
Phanerodontia, exhibiting 99.84 % similarity to Phanerodontia chrys­
osporium and 99.81 % similarity to Phanerodontia chrysosporium SILI, 
respectively.
Three strains were screened by the Congo red heating color method. 
The screened strains all exhibited relatively high cellulase activities in 
the culture medium, which were 5.49 U/mL, 5.26 U/mL, and 4.73 U/mL 
respectively. Through experiments on aniline blue medium and guaiacol 
medium, it was qualitatively verified that both strains S2 and S3 could 
produce laccase and lignin peroxidase, indicating their ability to 
degrade lignin. Preparation of spore suspension: The isolated strain was 
activated and inoculated onto PDA plates, which were then incubated at 
28 ◦C for 5–7 days. Once the colonies covered the entire medium sur­
face, spores were rinsed from the plate surface into an Erlenmeyer flask 
using sterile saline solution. The suspension was shaken at 120 r/min for 
3 h, followed by spore counting using a hemocytometer (Hennechart- 
Collette et al., 2014), and the concentration of the bacterial suspension 
of each strain was adjusted to 108 CFU/mL with sterile distilled water as 
the initial inoculation dose for the pretreatment. Throughout the 18-day 
pretreatment period, this initial dose ensured a substantial and active 
microbial population to initiate straw decomposition, with the subse­
quent dynamics driven by microbial growth and metabolic activity on 
the straw substrate.
2.2. Experimental design
This study was conducted in three sequential phases to systemati­
cally evaluate the pretreatment of rice straw. The basic pretreatment 
procedure for all batches was as follows: 5 g of rice straw was added into 
110 mL of deionized water, and then sterilized at 121 ◦C for 15 min in an 
autoclave (Model 2018-B3285, 30 L capacity, Shanghai Boxun Medical 
Biological Instrument Corp, China). Subsequently, specific microor­
ganisms and/or MNBs modifiers were added as described below, fol­
lowed by 18 days of pretreatment prior to anaerobic digestion.
Phase I: Screening of Microbial Consortium Ratios.
This phase aimed to identify the most effective ratio of the three 
strains (S1, S2, S3) without MNBs augmentation. H-1, H-2, H-3 groups: 
received 60 mL of mixed microbial suspension (108CFU/mL) at ratios of 
S1:S2:S3 =
(1:1:1; Balanced), (2:1:1; Bacterium-Enhanced), and 
(1:2.5:2.5; Fungus-Dominated), respectively. Control (CK): received 60 
mL of sterile deionized water instead of microbial suspension.
Phase II: Augmentation of the Optimal Consortium with Air-MNBs.
Based on the results of Phase I, this phase assessed the synergy be­
tween the optimal consortium and Air-MNBs. K-1, K-2, K-3 groups: 
corresponded to the same microbial ratios as H-1, H-2, and H-3, but 
pretreated with a mixture of 60 mL bacterial suspension and 100 mL Air- 
MNBs water. Control (CK-1): received 100 mL Air-MNBs water and 60 
mL sterile water without microbes.
Phase III: Comparison of MNBs Types on Functional Groups.
This phase dissected the effects of different MNBs types (Air vs. N₂) 
on the key functional units. A-1: S1 augmented with Air-MNBs; N-1: S1 
augmented with N₂-MNBs; A-2: fungal consortium (S2:S3 = 1:1) 
augmented with Air-MNBs; N-2: fungal consortium (S2:S3 = 1:1) 
augmented with N₂-MNBs. The pretreatment medium for all Phase III 
groups was 60 mL of the respective microbial suspension mixed with 
100 mL of the specified MNBs water.

MNBs Water Generation: MNBs water for all phases was prepared 
using a generator (ZJC-NM, Shanghai Zhongjing Environmental Pro­
tection Technology Co., Ltd.). Deionized water was aerated with com­
pressed air or N2 at 1.0 L/min for 30 min, producing bubbles primarily in 
the sub-micron range (100–800 nm) at a concentration of ~107–108 
particles/mL.
Anaerobic Digestion: Following the 18-day pretreatment, 100 mL of 
anaerobic inoculum was added to each reactor to initiate AD, during 
which gas production and digestate characteristics were monitored.
2.3. Analytical methods
The samples were heated to a constant weight at 105 ◦C and 600 ◦C, 
respectively, to measure the total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS). The 
cellulose content was determined by the sulfuric acid-potassium di­
chromate oxidation method. The hemicellulose content was measured 
by the dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) colorimetric method after hydrolysis 
with 2 mol/L HCl. The lignin content was determined by the sulfuric 
acid washing method (Chen et al., 2019).
To test various indicators of the straw hydrolysate, the samples were 
centrifuged (×14,000 rpm) and then filtered through a 0.45 μm filter 
membrane. The oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) was measured 
using an ORP meter (DZS-706-A, Leici, Shanghai). The soluble chemical 
oxygen demand (sCOD) was determined using the Hach rapid digestion 
method (DRB200 Hach digester, HACH Company, USA). The poly­
saccharide content was determined by the phenol-sulfuric acid method 
and the protein content was measured by the Coomassie Brilliant Blue G- 
250 spectrophotometric method. The concentrations of volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs) were quantified by gas chromatography (Agilent 7890) 
using a flame ionization detector (FID) and an HP-5 capillary column 
(30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.25 μm). The operational parameters were as 
follows: helium carrier gas at 1.0 mL/min, an injector temperature of 
250 ◦C, and a detector temperature of 240 ◦C. A standard solution 
containing a mixture of VFAs (acetic acid, propionic acid, iso-butyric 
acid, butyric acid, iso-valeric acid, and valeric acid) was used.
The activities of extracellular enzymes in the fermentation broth 
were semi-quantitatively profiled using API ZYM test strips (bioM´erieux, 
France). Following the manufacturer’s guidelines with modifications, 
the supernatant of the sample was obtained by centrifugation at 12,000 
rpm for 20 min and subsequent filtration through a 0.45 μm membrane. 
Then, 65 μL of the prepared supernatant was inoculated into each cupule 
of the API ZYM strip. The strips were incubated at 37 ◦C for 4 h in a 
humidified chamber to prevent evaporation. After incubation, ZYM A (a 
chromogenic reagent) and ZYM B (a pH-stabilizing reagent) were added 
sequentially to each cupule. The strips were then allowed to stand for 5 
min under strong light to allow for full color development. The resulting 
color in each cupule was immediately compared to the API ZYM refer­
ence chart. Enzyme activity was semi-quantitatively scored on a scale 
from 0 to 5, where 0 indicates no activity (colorless), 1 represents 5 nmol 
(very low), 2 represents 10 nmol (low), 3 represents 20 nmol (medium), 
4 represents 30 nmol (high), and 5 represents ≥40 nmol (very high) of 
hydrolyzed substrate.
2.4. Statistical analysis
All experimental data were obtained from triplicate trials and 
expressed as mean values with standard deviations (mean ± SD). Sta­
tistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 27.0, IBM, USA). 
For comparisons among multiple treatment groups (for example, mi­
crobial consortia ratios H-1 to H-3, MNBs-enhanced groups K-1 to K-3, 
and MNBs-type groups A-1/N-1/A-2/N-2), one-way analysis of variance 
(ANOVA) with Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) post-hoc 
test was applied. Significant differences were determined at p < 0.05. 
Similarly, Tukey’s HSD post hoc test was employed to analyze differ­
ences in straw degradation parameters (including TS, VS, cellulose, 
hemicellulose, and lignin contents) and methane production. 
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was performed to examine re­
lationships between key operational parameters (polysaccharides, pro­
teins, and sCOD concentrations) and methane production across 
different time points. Principal component analysis (PCA) was per­
formed to visualize the multivariate effects of different treatments 
(MNBs types and microbial consortia ratios) on overall system perfor­
mance. The statistical significance thresholds were set as: p < 0.05 
(significant), p < 0.01 (highly significant), p < 0.001 (extremely sig­
nificant). Graphical representations were generated using Origin 
(version 2024, OriginLab, USA).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Straw hydrolysis in biological pretreatment with single strains VS. 
compound microbial agent
The hydrolysis performance of straw pretreated with single or mixed 
microbial consortia was evaluated based on the reduction rates of TS and 
VS. As illustrated in Fig. 1a, all single-strain treatments significantly 
enhanced straw degradation compared to the control group, with strain 
S2 exhibiting the highest degradation rate of 11.0 %, slightly superior to 
strain S3 (9.0 %) and markedly higher than strain S1 (6.0 %). This dif­
ference can be attributed to the more efficient, substrate-specific syn­
ergy of fungal-derived cellulases and hemicellulases, where fungi 
maintain lignocellulose degradation capability through hydrolytic 
enzyme-dominated systems even under hypoxic conditions, while bac­
terial degradation typically depends on aerobic environments (Rollig 
et al., 2025). These findings align with previous studies demonstrating 
fungi’s superior lignocellulose degradation efficiency over bacteria in 
agricultural waste treatment systems. Combined with experimental data 
and operational conditions, the results clearly indicate that strains S2 
and S3 possess stronger lignocellulose matrix degradation capacity than 
S1. Based on these findings, experimental designs incorporating varying 
ratios of bacterial-fungal co-cultures could be implemented to investi­
gate potential synergistic enhancement of straw degradation efficiency.
To evaluate the pretreatment effects of bacterial-fungal consortia 
with different ratios on straw, the degradation rates of TS and VS by 
mixed strains are presented in Fig. 1b. Comparative analysis with single- 
strain pretreatment results (Fig. 1a) reveals that the mixed consortia 
significantly enhanced straw hydrolysis efficiency. The degradation of 
both TS and VS was monitored, providing complementary insights. The 
TS reduction reflects the overall mass loss including inorganic compo­
nents, while VS reduction specifically indicates the biodegradation of 
organic matter. Notably, the maximum TS degradation rates reached 
27.5 %, 22.5 %, and 19.0 % for H-2, H-3, and H-1, respectively, with H-2 
being significantly higher than both H-3 and H-1 (p < 0.05). The VS 
degradation is not prominent enough (Fig. 1b), confirming that the mass 
loss was primarily due to the consumption of organic components. This 
trend reveals that overall degradation efficiency depends on a balanced 
synergy between the fungal and bacterial components, rather than 
merely on the total fungal proportion.
The underlying functional specialization is elucidated in Fig. 1c, 
which shows the component-specific degradation rates. Due to the 
inherent laccase production characteristics of Phanerodontia sp. (Luo 
et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019), the highest lignin degradation rate was 
found in the fungal-dominated consortium H-3 (35.5 %), which was 
significantly greater than all other groups (p < 0.01). A more nuanced 
finding is that the H-2 consortium achieved a significantly higher lignin 
degradation rate (25.1 %) than H-1 (22.8 %) (p < 0.05), despite a lower 
nominal fungal inoculum ratio (1/2 in H-2 vs. 2/3 in H-1). This apparent 
paradox underscores that microbial synergy, not just inoculum size, 
governs function. In the H-2 ratio, the larger initial population of Bacillus 
velezensis (S1) may enhance the ligninolytic activity of the fungi by 
rapidly consuming and removing soluble sugars and intermediate me­
tabolites released during the initial breakdown of straw. This bacterial 
“scavenging” could prevent the catabolite repression of fungal

lignocellulolytic enzymes and maintain a microenvironment that is 
more favorable for fungal activity, thereby increasing the overall effi­
ciency of lignin decomposition. Conversely, the cellulose degradation 
efficiency was highest in H-2, indicating that this bacterium-enhanced 
consortium had a stronger ability to decompose cellulose, which can 
be attributed to the cellulolytic enzymes of Bacillus sp. (Dong et al., 
2024).
These findings demonstrate that the H-2 consortium achieved the 
best overall performance by fostering a synergistic partnership where 
bacterial activity potentiated fungal lignin degradation while concur­
rently executing robust cellulose hydrolysis. The experiment confirms 
that formulating microbial consortia with complementary functional 
ratios can significantly promote the degradation of key straw compo­
nents (Wu et al., 2022).
3.2. Enhanced hydrolysis of straw in biological pretreatment augmented 
with micro-nano bubbles
The synergistic effects of compound microbial agents augmented 
with MNBs (Air and N2, respectively) were explored. As shown in 
Fig. 2a, with the augmentation of Air-MNBs, the maximum reduction of 
TS (43.5 %) and VS (28 %) was found in the K-2 group, which was 
significantly higher than both K-1 and K-3 (p < 0.05 for both TS and VS). 
When comparing K group and H group with the same composite mi­
crobial agents, the degradation rates of VS were improved by 12.0 %, 
13.0 % and 17.1 % for the compound microbial agents H-1, H-2 and H-3, 
respectively. This enhancement in organic matter (VS) removal was 
consistent with the trends in Total Solids (TS) reduction. Furthermore, 
this study investigated the effects of different types of MNBs water (Air 
or N2) on the biological pretreatment with bacteria or fungi. For the 
bacterial pretreatment with S1, Air-MNBs (A-1) yielded significantly 
higher TS and VS degradation rates compared to N₂-MNBs (N-1) (p <
0.01, Fig. 2a, b). Furthermore, For the fungal pretreatment with S2 and 
S3, a significant difference of VS degradation rate was similarly found 
between Air-MNBs (12.0 %) and N2-MNBs (7.4 %). These results 
demonstrate the prominent augmentation effect of Air-MNBs on straw 
biodegradation(He et al., 2022).
Variations of sCOD and ORP in different treatment groups were 
monitored (Fig. c–f). With the increase in treatment time, the dynamic 
changes of dissolved oxygen and the release of reaction fermentation 
products may both affect the ORP (Wang et al., 2020). The significantly 
lower ORP in fungal-inoculated reactors (A-2 and N-2) is consistent with 
the high oxygen consumption rates typically associated with dense 
fungal mycelial networks. This creates a microaerobic to anaerobic 
microenvironment that can selectively favor certain lignocellulolytic 
enzymes, particularly those produced by white-rot fungi like Phaner­
odontia chrysosporium that maintain activity under oxygen-limited 
conditions (Etemadi-Khah and Pourbabaee, 2025; Lambooij et al., 
2017; Xiong et al., 2022). The stable, moderated ORP profiles observed 
in MNBs-augmented systems (Fig. 2e–f) suggest that MNBs help main­
tain a balanced redox environment, potentially preventing the complete 
oxygen depletion that could stall aerobic degradation processes. It is also 
noteworthy that while the maximum VS reduction rate was observed in 
A-1, the highest sCOD level was found in N-1. This result is also corre­
sponding to the previous statement, the stimulated activity of cellulose- 
decomposing bacteria also leads to the consumption of some soluble 
glucose (Sutaoney et al., 2024). In fact, special attention should be paid 
to the recovery rate of hydrolysis products, as it is usually directly 
proportional to the methane production in the subsequent digestion 
process.
Although a direct control with conventional macrobubbles was not 
included, the significant enhancements observed are likely attributable 
to the unique properties of MNBs. Unlike macrobubbles that rapidly 
escape the liquid, MNBs provide sustained gas transfer and can generate 
reactive oxygen species upon collapse (Xiao et al., 2025; Chuenchart 
et al., 2021). The stable, moderated ORP profiles (Fig. e-f) and the 
substantial increases in methane yield support the role of these MNBs- 
specific mechanisms, which cannot be achieved by short-lived 
macrobubbles.
3.3. Methane production potential test of straw after biological 
pretreatment
The influence of the combination of MNBs and mixed microbial 
agents on AD was further evaluated by the methane production potential 
test, which lasted from 7 days to 14 days. Fig. 3a presents the methane 
yield from straw pretreated with composite microbial consortia. The H-2 
consortium demonstrated the highest methane production at 35.5 mL/g 
VS, representing an 8-fold increase over the control, followed by H-3 at 
15.1 mL/g VS. The H-1 consortium yielded the lowest methane pro­
duction, which is a direct consequence of its inferior pretreatment per­
formance, as shown by its lowest VS degradation rate (Fig. 1b) and 
cellulose degradation efficiency (Fig. 1c). The daily progression of 
methane production for all pretreatment groups, which further illus­
trates the differential startup and accumulation patterns, is provided in 
Fig. S2 (Supplementary Information). The strong correlation between 
solids degradation during pretreatment and ultimate methane yield 
underscores that the primary role of the microbial consortia is to create 
bioavailable substrates for the anaerobic community. These production 
trends validate the conclusion from Section 3.1 that a balanced synergy 
(as achieved in H-2), rather than a simply high fungal proportion, is 
crucial for optimizing the entire process from straw decomposition to 
biomethane production. This pattern aligns with the “fungal-dominated 
decomposition and bacterial-mediated exploitation” model (Miao et al., 
2025), wherein the fungi primarily break down the complex lignocel­
lulose, and the bacteria, in a complementary role, facilitate the con­
version of intermediates to ultimately promote methanogenesis. The 
balanced ratio in H-2/K-2 optimally harnesses this synergy, leading to 
superior system performance (Thongbunrod and Chaiprasert, 2022).
Fig. 3b and c compared the cumulative methane production from 
straw pretreated with Air-MNBs and N2-MNBs. As shown, the K-2 group 
(S1:S2:S3 = 2:1:1) achieved the highest methane production at 47.5 mL/

g VS, which was significantly greater than that of K-3 and K-1 (p < 0.01). 
Notably, the introduction of Air-MNBs enhanced methane yields by 
34.2 %, 34.0 % and 47.7 %, respectively, with the same ratio of mixed 
microbial agents. Meanwhile, as seen in Fig. 3c, for the bacterial pre­
treatment (S1), the methane yield with Air-MNBs (A-1, 31.1 mL/g VS) 
was significantly higher than with N₂-MNBs (N-1, 26.5 mL/g VS) (p <
0.05). Similarly, for the fungal pretreatment (S2:S3), Air-MNBs (A-2) 
also led to a significantly greater methane yield compared to N₂-MNBs 
(N-2) (p < 0.05).
Generally, these improvements correlate well with the VS degrada­
tion rates during the pretreatment phase. The incorporation of Air-MNBs 
has been demonstrated to significantly enhance methane yield in AD 
processes (Li et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018). This phenomenon is 
mechanistically explained by two distinctive properties of air-MNBs, i.e. 
their superior mass transfer efficiency and the potential to generate 
reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is hypothesized that the synergistic 
effects of ROS-induced mild oxidative disruption and enhanced mass 
transfer kinetics facilitate the hydrolysis of macromolecular organic 
substrates (particularly polysaccharides and proteins), consequently 
increasing VFAs production (Yamaguchi et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2017; 
Zhou et al., 2025). Similar results are observed in this study, evidenced 
by the higher VFAs level in A-1 and A-2 as compared to N-1 and N2. The 
comprehensive time-course profiles of polysaccharides, proteins, and 
VFAs that underpin this conclusion are detailed in Fig. S3

A pivotal finding emerged when we specifically interrogated the role 
of MNBs. The strength of the positive correlation between VFAs-5 and 
methane yield was significantly more pronounced in the Air-MNBs 
augmented groups compared to the non-MNBs controls. This provides 
direct statistical evidence that Air-MNBs enhance the metabolic con­

nism of the observed synergy. The marked strengthening of correlations

that MNBs promote methane production by optimizing the intermediate 
metabolism throughout the digestion process (Hou et al., 2025; Zhang

3.4. Analysis of enzyme activity of straw pretreated by composite 
microbial agents
The analysis of the enzyme activity of straw pretreated with a 
combination of MNBs and mixed microbial agents was conducted to 
examine the differences in enzyme activity among different types of 
MNBs. As shown in Fig. 5a, 11 extracellular enzymes were detected in 
both K-1 and K-2, while only 10 were found in K-3. All three groups 
shared eight enzymes: Alkaline phosphatase, Esterase(C4), Leucine 
arylamidase, trypsin, acid phosphatase, naphthol-AS-BI-phosphate hy­
drolase, α-glucosidase, and β-glucosidase—a rate-limiting enzyme in 
cellulose degradation that converts cellobiose to glucose, directly 
providing substrates for subsequent acidogenesis and methanogenesis. 
Notably, the detection of β-glucosidase, along with other cellulolytic (e. 
g., β-galactosidase) and ligninolytic enzymes, creates a complementary 
enzymatic portfolio that efficiently deconstructs the lignocellulosic 
matrix into fermentable sugars, which are precursors for VFAs and ul­
timately methane(Li et al., 2021). The enhanced diversity and activity of 
these key hydrolytic enzymes in MNBs-assisted groups, particularly 
β-glucosidase, correlates with the observed improvements in methane 
yield, suggesting MNBs create conditions favorable for the synthesis and 
secretion of enzymes critical for the AD feedstock preparation. No sig­
nificant difference was observed between K-1 and K-2 (p > 0.05), but 
significant differences were detected between K-2 and K-3 (p < 0.01) 
and between K-1 and K-3 (p < 0.01) (Wang and Li, 2016). The superior 
straw degradation efficiency and higher sCOD levels observed in the K-1 
and K-2 groups (Fig. 2a, c) can be attributed to this more diverse and 
balanced suite of hydrolytic enzymes, which facilitates a more 
comprehensive breakdown of the straw’s polymeric structure into 
fermentable sugars (Li et al., 2024).
Fig. 5b shows the extracellular enzyme heatmap of straw pretreated 
with air and N2-MNBs. It can be seen from the figure that the number of 
detectable enzyme activities in Groups A-1, A-2, N-1, and N-2 are 12, 10, 
12, and 10 respectively. α-Galactosidase and β-galactosidase were only 
detected in the system with the addition of strain S1. The detection of 
these hemicellulose-degrading (galactosidases) and cellulose-degrading 
(glucosidases) enzymes aligns with the functional roles of the inoculated 
strains and supports the component-specific degradation patterns shown 
in Fig. 1c. By comparison, the number of detectable enzyme activities of 
strain H1 (Bacillus) was significantly more than that of strains S2 and S3 
(Phanerodontia) (p < 0.01). Microbial cultivation analysis revealed that 
strains S1, S2, and S3 produced 3, 8, and 9 distinct extracellular en­
zymes, respectively. The analysis of extracellular enzymes provides 
crucial insights into the mechanistic role of MNBs.
While control groups without microbial inoculation showed negli­
gible enzyme activity, the profiling of experimental groups revealed that 
MNBs augmentation led to a significant enhancement in both the di­
versity and activity of extracellular enzymes compared to what is typi­
cally observed in standard microbial cultivations. The sustained and 
diverse enzyme activities detected throughout the pretreatment phase 
(Fig. 5) indicate that the inoculated microbial consortia not only 
remained viable but were functionally active, effectively colonizing the 
straw substrate. This enhancement is evident in two key aspects: First, 
the number of detectable enzyme types was higher in the optimal con­
sortia (e.g., 11 types in K-1 and K-2) compared to others (9 in K-3). 
Second, the overall enzyme activity levels were elevated in MNBs- 
assisted groups. Thus, the improvement can be attributed to the 
unique microenvironment induced by MNBs, such as elevated dissolved 
oxygen levels and the generation of mild oxidative stress, which can 
activate microbial stress responses and regulate gene expression, 
thereby promoting the synthesis and secretion of extracellular enzymes 
(Wang et al., 2024). Although the chemical properties of air and nitro­
gen differ, the similar enzyme response suggests that the upregulation is 
primarily driven by the shared physical effects of MNBs, including gas- 
liquid interface dynamics and associated shear forces.
The efficiency of the MNBs-microbial pretreatment approach can be 
contextualized by comparing it with conventional methods reported in 
the literature. For instance, chemical pretreatments like alkaline or acid 
(e.g., NaOH, H₂SO₄) treatments of rice straw typically achieve lignin 
degradation rates of 30–60 % but often generate inhibitory byproducts 
and require extensive washing, increasing operational costs and envi­
ronmental impact (Anacleto et al., 2024; Tulun and Bilgin, 2019). 
Physical methods such as steam explosion can achieve high cellulose 
accessibility but are energy-intensive. In comparison, the present MNBs- 
microbial pretreatment achieved a 43.5 % TS degradation and a 47.5 
mL/g VS methane yield, which is competitive with or superior to many 
conventional methods. For example, a study on fungal pretreatment of 
rice straw with Phanerochaete chrysosporium alone reported a methane 
yield of ~35 mL/g VS (Shah et al., 2025), while the MNBs augmentation 
here pushed the yield significantly higher. The principal advantage of 
the MNBs approach lies in its operational simplicity, minimal chemical 
input, and synergistic enhancement of biological activity, offering a 
more sustainable alternative.
The findings of this study extend beyond a technical demonstration, 
offering insights into synergistic mechanisms and prompting consider­
ation of real-world application. The superior performance of MNBs- 
augmented pretreatment is attributed to a combination of physical 
and chemical effects. While enhanced oxygen mass transfer is a key 
factor, the unique properties of MNBs, such as their surface charge and 
the generation of ROS during collapse, likely play crucial roles. These 
properties can improve microbial-substrate contact efficiency and 
induce mild oxidative disruption of the lignocellulosic matrix, thereby 
facilitating enzymatic attack. The altered extracellular enzyme profiles 
observed in this study support the view of MNBs as biochemical mod­
ulators. Translating this technology to an industrial scale requires 
addressing its practical feasibility. The primary consideration is the 
energy cost of MNBs generation, which must be weighed against the 
significant gains in methane yield and potential reductions in pretreat­
ment time. A major advantage lies in its straightforward integration as a 
pre-treatment “booster” for existing anaerobic digesters, while mini­
mizing infrastructural changes. Future research should prioritize pilot- 
scale trials to validate long-term stability and conduct detailed techno- 
economic analyses, comparing this green approach against conven­
tional, often more energy-intensive or chemically intensive, pretreat­
ment methods.
4. Conclusions
In conclusion, this study establishes that augmenting designed mi­
crobial consortia with Air-MNBs presents a highly effective and novel 
strategy for pretreating rice straw, leading to dramatically enhanced 
anaerobic digestion performance. The consortium with a balanced ratio 
(K-2, S1:S2:S3 = 2:1:1) achieved the most pronounced synergy, resulting 
in the highest degradation of total solids (43.5 %) and volatile solids 
(28.0 %), and a maximum methane yield of 47.5 mL/g VS. The pre­
treatment efficacy was highly dependent on the microbial composition; 
Air-MNBs provided a more substantial boost to the bacterial pretreat­
ment, whereas their effect on the fungal consortium was less distinct but

viability of this integrated and promising pretreatment technology.
